svg.title: The human heart in frontal section
svg.desc: Frontal section of the human heart showing the four chambers, the septum, the atrioventricular and semilunar valves with chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, the venae cavae, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta, a coronary artery and the conducting system, with blood flow shown in blue (deoxygenated) and red (oxygenated).
svg.text: Viewed from the front: the left side of the heart is on the right of the diagram.

g.data-info: Pulmonary trunk and its right and left branches: carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs (the only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood after birth).
Carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium (four in humans; two are drawn).

Largest artery: carries oxygenated blood at high pressure from the left ventricle to the body. Its elastic wall stretches and recoils with each beat. The arch gives off three branches to the head and arms.
Returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms to the right atrium.
Returns deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium.
Pulmonary trunk and its right and left branches: carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs (the only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood after birth).
Muscular wall separating the left and right sides, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. Carries the bundle of His.
Receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the venae cavae. Thin muscular wall: it only pumps blood a short distance into the right ventricle. Contains the SA node.
Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins and pumps it into the left ventricle.
Pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Its wall is thinner than the left ventricle’s because the lungs are close and lung capillaries need low pressure.
Thickest wall of the heart: it generates the high pressure needed to pump oxygenated blood through the aorta to the whole body. Forms the apex.
Muscles of the ventricle wall that contract with the ventricle, tightening the chordae tendineae.
Three cusps between the right atrium and right ventricle. Open when atrial pressure is higher; pushed shut when the ventricle contracts, preventing backflow into the atrium.
Two cusps between the left atrium and left ventricle; closes during ventricular systole to stop backflow into the atrium.
Tendinous cords joining the cusps of the AV valves to papillary muscles; they stop the cusps turning inside out into the atria when the ventricles contract.
Three pocket-shaped cusps at the base of the pulmonary artery. Open while the right ventricle ejects blood; close when ventricular pressure falls, preventing backflow into the ventricle.
Three pocket-shaped cusps at the base of the aorta; prevent backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole.
Branches from the base of the aorta and supplies the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood. Blockage (occlusion) causes a heart attack.
The pacemaker: specialised muscle cells in the right atrium wall that fire impulses spontaneously (myogenic), starting each heartbeat. The impulse spreads through both atria, which contract.
Delays the impulse by about 0.1 s so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract, then passes it to the bundle of His.

g.data-name: Bundle of His and Purkinje fibres
g.data-info: Conducting fibres that carry the impulse down the septum to the apex and up through the ventricle walls, so the ventricles contract from the apex upwards, squeezing blood towards the arteries.
g.aria-label: Bundle of His and Purkinje fibres

g.text: Bundle of His and Purkinje fibres

svg.text: Blue: deoxygenated blood. Red: oxygenated blood. Yellow: conducting system. Not to scale.

g.text: Atrial systole: SA node fires; atria contract; AV valves open
Ventricular systole: AV valves shut; semilunar valves open; blood ejected
Diastole: semilunar valves shut; AV valves open; chambers fill
